title: Overcoming the Quasi-Static Bottleneck: A Finite-Time Quantum Otto Information Engine Achieving Near-Unity Efficiency
abstract: Generally, quantum heat engines driven by Gibbs reservoirs achieve their maximum work and efficiency only in quasi-static processes, a constraint that hampers practical applications due to the resulting vanishing power output. To address this fundamental limitation, we propose a finite-time quantum Otto information engine (OIE) driven by a Maxwell's demon paired with a single Gibbs reservoir. We demonstrate that the demon's measurement and feedback control can preserve quantum coherence to extract coherent work, while harnessing quantum internal friction as a work source. Consequently, the OIE can produce work by only modulating the eigenstates of the Hamiltonian, and surpass the quasi-static limits of its conventional counterpart in the work output and the efficiency, which accounts for the energetic cost of the demon. Notably, the OIE can achieve near-perfect efficiency alongside positive work extraction in the rapid-driving regime.
summary: This paper proposes a Quantum Otto Information Engine (OIE) to overcome the fundamental limitation that quantum heat engines can only operate efficiently in the slow, quasi-static limit. By incorporating a Maxwell's demon for measurement and feedback control, the OIE successfully extracts work and maintains high efficiency even when driven rapidly. This demonstrates a pathway for building high-performance, non-equilibrium quantum machines.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is overcoming the quasi-static bottleneck in quantum heat engines, which severely limits their practical power output.
main_result: The proposed Quantum Otto Information Engine (OIE) surpasses the quasi-static limits of conventional engines, achieving near-perfect efficiency alongside positive work extraction even in the rapid-driving regime.
method: The authors analyze the engine cycle by replacing the standard isochoric heating stroke with a process involving a Maxwell's demon's measurement and state-dependent feedback control.
model_or_system: The model is a quantum Otto engine cycle applied to a spin-1/2 particle, utilizing a single Gibbs reservoir and incorporating the information processing steps of a Maxwell's demon.
key_observables: Efficiency ($\eta$), work output ($W$), quantum coherence ($C(ho)$), and quantum mutual information ($I$).
important_parameters: Measurement error ($\epsilon$), driving time ($	au$), and the comparison to quasi-static limits.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the demon's energy cost is accounted for, and specific conditions are derived for achieving zero heat dissipation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic cycles (OHE vs. OIE) and plot work and efficiency versus driving time ($	au$) and measurement error ($\epsilon$), demonstrating performance improvements.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitations of the conventional Otto Heat Engine (OHE) in finite time. It then introduces the OIE, detailing how the demon's measurement and feedback mechanism modifies the cycle. Finally, it analyzes the performance in the rapid-driving regime to prove the theoretical advantages of the OIE.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles non-equilibrium thermodynamics by integrating information theory (Maxwell's Demon) into energy conversion cycles, which is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems and quantum thermodynamics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic diagrams of the finite time quantum Otto heat engine (OHE) (a) and quantum Otto information engine (OIE) (b). (a) The conventional quantum OHE undergoes four steps: adiabatic compression (ρt0 →ρt1), isochoric heating (ρt1 →ρt2) at inverse temperature βh with absorbing heat Qh, adiabatic expansion (ρt2 →ρt3) and isochoric cooling (ρt3 →ρt0) at inverse temperature βc with absorbing heat Qc. (b) In the quantum OIE, the isochoric heating stroke is replaced by a demon’s measurement Me,g followed by state-dependent feedback control, represented by the identity operator I and the Pauli operator σx.

FIG. 2. (a) The transition probability ξ, along with (b) the work output W and (c) the efficiency η of the finite-time quantum OHE as functions of the driving time τ. The chosen simulation parameters are γ0 = 10, βc = 10βh = 1, ωh = 5ωc = 5, and τc = 10τh = 2. Under this parameter regime, the damping factor evaluates to e−Γcτc ≈1.6 × 10−19, which ensures that the working system fully relaxes back to its initial Gibbs state at the end of each cycle, thereby maintaining a strictly closed cyclic operation.

FIG. 3. Quantum coherence of the OIE at times t1 and t2, along with the acquired quantum mutual information I, as functions of the measurement error ϵ for driving time τ = 0.1. The other parameters are the same Fig. 2.

FIG. 4. The output work and the efficiency of the finite time quantum OIE as functions of the driving time τ with given ωh under measurement error ϵ = 0.5. The other parameters are the same as Fig. 2.
